newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - US rates seen up ahead of Japan, Germany.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - US rates seen up ahead of Japan, Germany.

text.p: Interest rates in the United States are expected to rise before those in Japan and Germany as the Federal Reserve takes action to subdue price pressures in the economy, a Reuters survey showed on Monday.

Before the end of this year, the Fed will raise the funds rate by 25 or 50 basis points from 5.25 percent, according to 16 out of 22 contributors to the survey. Most expect the rise before the end of June.
In contrast, only 11 expect a rise in Japanese interest rates and only five expect a rise in German rates before 1998.

"The U.S. economy is growing above trend and wage pressures are growing. Ultimately the Fed must raise rates to ward off a rise in consumer price inflation," said Teis Knuthsen, director of European analysis at First Chicago.
Eleven economists said they believed Japan's economy would recover sufficiently for a rise in the discount rate by between 25 and 50 basis points by December, from the current 0.5 percent.
"We think there will be a rise to support the yen and because the economy is not as weak as people think," said Adrian Owens, European economist at Julius Baer.
Investor appetite for U.S. assets has seen the dollar soar to below 125 yen recently, the highest since February 1993.
Eight economists gave a more pessimistic view on Japan's prospects for recovery, saying they expected no change in rates this year.

"The Japanese economy is sluggish and consumption tax will prompt more weakness. The crisis in the financial system is on-going and inflation remains low," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International.

The rise in consumption tax to five percent on April 1, 1997 from three percent was endorsed by the Japanese government last year. Many analysts expect the rise to weigh heavily on consumer confidence and expenditure.
Fiscal austerity and its effect on the German domestic economy is the major reason given by the 12 economists for expecting no change in German interest rates.

"With fiscal tightening ticking in, the only signs of recovery are in the export sector, but this is not feeding through into the domestic economy which remains very weak," said Mike Dicks, senior economist at Lehman Brothers.
"Growth will be very important this year, to get deficits down to the levels set in the Maastricht criteria."
Countries aiming to qualify for European economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999 must reduce their 1997 budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product.

To achieve that target, Germany's economy must grow substantially to boost government revenues, analysts say. Raising interest rates is not going to help the economy meet the convergence criteria, they said.
Five contributors expect the German discount and lombard rates to be raised to 3.5 and five percent from three and 4.5 percent respectively by quarter four 1997.
However, five expect the discount rate to be reduced by 50 basis points before the end of the year.

"The German economy is still sluggish. The recovery was export-led, but domestic demand remains stagnant. Unemployment is at record highs, monetary growth is set to slow and inflation is low," said DKB's Stamenkovic.
German unemployment rose to an unadjusted 4.148 million from 3.942 million in November. The unadjusted jobless rate rose to 10.8 percent in December from 10.3 percent.
